transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in today?

Well, nice to meet you, Doc. I guess what brings me in is I just keep messing up these little things. Like, I was at the senior center the other day, and I wrote the wrong time down on the class sheet. It was for a history thing. I never really thought I'd be hanging around a senior center, to be honest with you. Seems like just yesterday I was still out working, but you know how time flies. My buddy Frank convinced me to go, he says they have good donuts. The donuts were actually pretty stale, but... anyway, yeah, it's just little mistakes like that. Or I'll be out in the garage, measuring a board once, and I'll still cut it a hair short because I just sort of skipped over the small print on the tape measure. Which is really frustrating because lumber isn't cheap right now. You go to the hardware store these days and a simple piece of pine costs you an arm and a leg. I remember when you could get a whole truckload for what they charge for a few planks now. But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, why I'm here. Just... making those little errors, I guess.
Do you ever forget recent events, like conversations or things you did earlier in the day?

Forget things from earlier? No, not really. My memory for that kind of stuff is actually pretty sharp. Like, just this morning I was talking to my neighbor, Bob, over the fence, and I remember it clear as day. He was telling me his lawnmower is acting up again. It's one of those riding ones, a John Deere. Nice machine, green and yellow, but you know, they just don't make them like they used to. Back in the day, if your mower broke, you just took a wrench to it, maybe cleaned out the carburetor, and you were good to go. Now? Everything's got a computer in it. I don't know why a lawnmower needs a microchip. It just cuts grass! You take it to the shop and they charge you two hundred bucks just to plug it into a diagnostic machine. It's an absolute racket, if you ask me. Bob was saying he might just buy a push mower and be done with it, get some exercise. His wife would probably like that, she's always telling him to get off the couch. But... anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, memory. No, I don't forget conversations or what I did that day. I remember all that just fine.
Have you noticed that your thinking or memory is worse now than it used to be?

Worse than it used to be? No, I wouldn't say that. My memory's always been about the same, really. I mean, I can still remember the starting lineup for the '86 Mets. What a season that was. You don't see baseball played like that anymore, with real grit, you know? Now it's all about launch angles and analytics. They've got these guys swinging for the fences every time, striking out a hundred and fifty times a year and nobody bats an eye. Back when I played a little ball in high school—nothing fancy, just varsity—coach would've benched you for a week if you swung at some of the garbage these pros go after today. You had to protect the plate. We had this field behind the old middle school, and the grass was always cut way too high, so grounders would just die in the infield. You really had to leg it out. But, uh... sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, my thinking getting worse. No, no, I think my brain's working just about the same as it always has. Just... still missing those little details, like I said.
Have these mistakes started interfering with your day-to-day activities?

Well, yeah, I guess they have. It's kind of embarrassing, really. Like, I used to help lead these DIY workshops at the community center, you know? Just basic stuff—building birdhouses, fixing leaky faucets, that sort of thing. I always liked working with my hands. My dad taught me how to use a hammer before I could even ride a bike. He was a carpenter, old school. Built our whole back deck himself over a couple of weekends. He used this heavy cedar wood, smelled fantastic. You don't see decks built like that anymore, everything's that composite plastic stuff now. Supposed to last forever, they say, but it just looks fake to me. It gets hotter than a frying pan in the summer, too. You walk out there barefoot and you'll burn your soles right off. Dad always said wood breathes, it has character. He had this old Stanley hand plane that he cherished... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, the workshops. Yeah, I had to step back from leading those because I kept mixing up the measurements on the handouts or forgetting which tools we needed for the day. And my wife, she's been having to double-check all our plans lately. Otherwise, I end up writing down the wrong day or time, and I almost threw off a visit with our grandkids last month. We were supposed to go to the zoo, but I told them Sunday instead of Saturday. The zoo is crazy on Sundays, anyway. Too many strollers. But yeah, she has to check behind me now so I don't mess up our family stuff or the things we do at the center.
Have these kinds of mistakes been something you've had for as long as you can remember, or are they new in the past few years?

No, it's definitely not new. It's been like this for as long as I can remember, honestly. I mean, even back in elementary school, my teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright, but I'd always forget my books or lose my homework. And I'd just stare out the window half the day unless someone was there to keep me on track. I remember my fifth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable. She had this huge collection of ceramic frogs on her desk. Hundreds of them, all different sizes. Some of them had little umbrellas, some were playing instruments. It was the strangest thing. One time, Billy Henderson accidentally knocked over the one playing the banjo, and she made him stay after school for a week to glue it back together. Billy was always getting into trouble, though. He ended up moving to Ohio a few years later. I always wondered what happened to him. We used to trade baseball cards behind the bleachers. He had a rookie Mickey Mantle that was in terrible shape, corners all bent up, but he treated it like it was gold. I tried to trade him my whole binder for it once, but he wouldn't budge. Anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the mistakes. Yeah, no, it's not a new thing at all. It's just how I've always been.
Have these mistakes been getting progressively worse over time?

Progressively worse? Well, I wouldn't say they're getting worse, like, overall. It's more that it's been noticeably interfering with things since we moved into the condo. That was about a year and a month ago. We downsized, you know? The old house was just too much to keep up with. The gutters alone were a nightmare. Every fall, the oak tree in the front yard would just dump leaves everywhere. I used to get up on this rickety old aluminum ladder to clean them out. My wife hated it when I did that. She was always convinced I was going to break my neck. And honestly, she wasn't wrong to worry. One time, the ladder slipped in the mud and I ended up dangling from the gutter like some kind of action hero. Ripped the whole gutter right off the fascia board. Took me three weekends to fix that mess, had to borrow my neighbor's truck to get the new siding from the hardware store. He had this beautiful old Chevy C10, step-side bed, painted cherry red. Handled like a boat, but man, did it have style. They don't make trucks like that anymore, all steel and chrome. Now they're basically luxury cars with a bed attached. Heated steering wheels, backup cameras... who needs a backup camera to park a truck? You just use your mirrors. Anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, getting worse. No, I don't think it's getting worse, just... more noticeable since we moved into the condo last year. Less space, so my wife sees every little thing I forget now.
Has anyone who knows you well noticed that your memory or thinking has clearly gotten worse?

Well, no, not that my thinking is getting worse, exactly. My wife just says I'm the same old scatterbrain I've always been. She calls it my "selective attention," which I think is a bit unfair. I mean, I pay attention to things, just... maybe not the things she wants me to. Like last week, she asked me to pick up milk, and I completely forgot, but I did notice that the grocery store had rearranged their entire produce section. They moved the apples to where the citrus used to be, and honestly, the lighting over there is terrible for apples. It makes the Red Delicious look almost purple. I asked the produce manager about it—nice kid, name tag said 'Kevin'—and he said it was corporate policy. Corporate policy for apples! Can you imagine? The suits sitting in some office in Chicago deciding where the Granny Smiths should go in a store in our town. It's ridiculous. Kevin agreed with me, though. He said he misses the old layout. He’s going to college for business, actually, wants to open his own bakery someday. His grandmother taught him how to make sourdough from a starter she’s had since the seventies. You know how hard it is to keep a starter alive that long? You have to feed it like a pet. My sister tried it once during the pandemic, and it smelled like old gym socks within a week. She ended up throwing it out and just buying the frozen dinner rolls... wait, what did you ask me? 

Oh, right, if anyone noticed my memory getting worse. No, no one's said it's getting worse. Just the same as it's always been, really.
When you were a child, did teachers or parents often describe you as distractible or having trouble staying on task?

Well, I'm not really sure if they used those exact words, but yeah, they definitely noticed. Like I said, Mrs. Gable used to say I'd stare out the window. My mom was always getting on me about not finishing my chores, too. She'd tell me to clean my room, and I'd start, but then I'd find an old comic book under my bed and just sit there reading it for an hour. I had this huge stack of Archie comics. Jughead was always my favorite, the way he could eat all those hamburgers. I never understood how he afforded them, though. Pops Chock'lit Shoppe must have been giving him a serious discount. Or maybe he just had a tab he never paid. You know, diners used to do that back in the day. You could just run a tab and settle up on payday. Try doing that at a McDonald's now, they'd look at you like you were crazy. Everything's so impersonal now, just tap your card and go. I miss the days when the waitress knew your name and how you liked your coffee. There was this place downtown, The Silver Spoon, they made the best cherry pie. The crust was so flaky... 

Sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? What was the question? Oh, right, distractible. Yeah, I don't know if they called it that, but I definitely had trouble sticking to what I was supposed to be doing.
